statement.p: A voltage V across a resistance R generates a current I=V/R. If a constant voltage of 12 volts is put across a resistance that is increasing at a rate of 0.3 ohms per second when the resistance is 8 ohms, at what rate is the current changing? (Give .)

static.solution: dR/dt=0.3 when R=8 and V=12 and we want to know dI/dt. Differentiating I=V/R with V constant gives \frac{dI}{dt}=V\left(-\frac{1}{R^2}\frac{dR}{dt}\right), so substituting gives \frac{dI}{dt}=12\left(-\frac{1}{8^2}\cdot 0.3\right) \approx -0.0563 \hbox{ amp/s }. (Note that we know the units are amp/s from the Leibnitz form of the derivative, dI\over dt. It is, of course, equally correct to use the expression on the right-hand side to determine the units, \left(\frac{\hbox{V}}{\hbox{ohm}{}^2}\right)\left(\frac{\hbox{ohm}}{\hbox{s}}\right), or, in homework-friendly form, V/ohm*s.)
